topics.title: Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead & Rate Limiting (Resilience4j)
topics.summary: Prevent cascading failures in microservices with stateful Circuit Breakers, thread pool bulkheads, and fallback mechanisms.
topics.interviewTip: Highlight the difference between COUNT_BASED (evaluates last N calls) and TIME_BASED sliding windows (evaluates calls in last N seconds).

topics.title: Saga Pattern: Choreography vs Orchestration
topics.summary: Maintain data consistency across microservices without 2PC using local transactions and compensating rollbacks.
topics.content:
## Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions

### Why 2-Phase Commit (2PC) Fails in Microservices
2PC requires all participating databases to hold locks until every node votes. If one service is slow, all database connections remain blocked. It violates microservice autonomy and scalability.

### The Saga Architecture
A Saga is a sequence of **local transactions**. Each transaction updates data in a single service and publishes an event. If a step fails, the Saga executes **compensating transactions** in reverse to undo the preceding steps.

```
Forward Execution:
[Create Order] ──► [Charge Payment] ──► [Reserve Inventory] ──► [Complete]

Compensating Rollback (when Inventory fails):
[Cancel Order] ◄── [Refund Payment] ◄── [Inventory Out of Stock!]
```

### Choreography vs Orchestration

| Attribute | Choreography (Event-Driven) | Orchestration (Command-Driven) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Coordination** | Decentralized via Kafka domain events | Centralized coordinator (e.g. Camunda, Temporal) |
| **Coupling** | Loose coupling | Services depend on orchestrator interface |
| **Complexity** | Difficult to track flow (cyclic dependencies) | Clear single source of workflow state machine |
| **Best For** | Simple workflows (2-4 services) | Complex, multi-branch business workflows |
topics.interviewTip: Emphasize that Compensating Transactions must be Idempotent because network retries can cause compensation events to execute multiple times.

topics.title: Spring Cloud Gateway & Backend-For-Frontend (BFF) Pattern
topics.summary: Centralize cross-cutting concerns: Netty reactive routing, JWT validation filters, request decoration, and BFF design.
topics.content:
## API Gateway & Backend-For-Frontend (BFF)

### Why API Gateway?
Instead of mobile and web clients calling 20 individual microservices directly:
1. **Single Entry Point**: Shields internal microservice topology.
2. **Cross-Cutting Concerns**: Authentication, Rate Limiting, SSL termination, and CORS handled in one place.
3. **Protocol Translation**: Translates external HTTP/1.1 REST or WebSockets to internal gRPC or Kafka streams.

### Reactive Spring Cloud Gateway Configuration
Built on Project Reactor and Netty (non-blocking event loop):

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: order-service-route
          uri: lb://ORDER-SERVICE # Client-side load balancing via Eureka / Consul
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/v1/orders/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=2
            - AddRequestHeader=X-Gateway-Timestamp, #{T(System).currentTimeMillis()}
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100
                key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"
```

### The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) Pattern
Rather than building a single massive monolithic gateway for all clients:
- **Mobile BFF**: Returns lightweight payloads tailored for low mobile bandwidth (strips unneeded JSON fields).
- **Web BFF**: Aggregates multiple API calls into dense payloads for desktop browsers.
topics.interviewTip: Highlight that Spring Cloud Gateway is built on Netty (reactive non-blocking), completely replacing old blocking Netflix Zuul 1.x servlet architecture.

topics.title: Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry, TraceID & SpanID Propagation
topics.summary: Diagnose cross-service latency regressions by propagating W3C Trace Context, Span IDs, and MDC logging across threads.
topics.content:
## Distributed Tracing & OpenTelemetry

### Trace vs Span Architecture
- **Trace**: Represents the entire end-to-end journey of a single user request across 10 microservices. Identified by a unique **`TraceId`**.
- **Span**: Represents a single unit of work within a service (e.g. an HTTP call, SQL query, Kafka publish). Identified by a unique **`SpanId`** and parent **`ParentSpanId`**.

```
[Trace ID: 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736]
├── [Span 1: API Gateway (25ms)]
│   └── [Span 2: Order Service (80ms)]
│       ├── [Span 3: PostgreSQL Query 'SELECT *' (12ms)]
│       └── [Span 4: Payment Client Feign (65ms)]
│           └── [Span 5: Payment Gateway Service (50ms)]
```

### W3C Trace Context Standard (`traceparent` header)
Services communicate trace context over HTTP using the standardized `traceparent` header:
```http
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
              │  └────────── Trace ID ──────────┘ └─ Span ID ─┘ └Flags
              Version
```

### Correlating Logs via SLF4J MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context)
Spring Boot 3 + Micrometer Tracing automatically populates MDC values so every log line contains the TraceId:

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml -->
<pattern>%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [%thread] [TraceId=%X{traceId}] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
```
Now pasting a single `TraceId` into Grafana Loki or ELK pulls up logs from all 10 microservices simultaneously!
topics.interviewTip: Explain MDC context propagation across asynchronous thread boundaries (CompletableFuture, Executors): MDC is backed by ThreadLocal, so async executors require ContextSnapshot or TaskDecorator.

topics.title: Service Discovery: Eureka & Client-Side Load Balancing
topics.summary: Enable dynamic service-to-service calls using Eureka registry, heartbeat-based health checks, and client-side load balancing via Spring Cloud LoadBalancer.
topics.content:
## Service Discovery: Eureka & Client-Side Load Balancing

### Why Static Service URLs Fail
In a dynamic cloud environment, service instances scale up/down, crash, and restart with new IP addresses constantly. Hardcoding `http://payment-service:8081` breaks the moment that instance dies.

### Registry-Based vs DNS-Based Discovery

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Service Registry (Eureka)           │
│  payment-service → [10.0.1.5:8081, 10.0.1.6:8081]│
│  order-service   → [10.0.1.9:8080]              │
└──────────┬─────────────────────────────┬────────┘
           │ Register + Heartbeat        │ Fetch Registry
           ▼                             ▼
    [payment-service]            [order-service]
    (every 30s heartbeat)        (cache refreshed every 30s)
```

**Registry-based** (Eureka, Consul): Services self-register with metadata. Clients fetch the full registry and cache it locally. Load balancing decision stays on the client.

**DNS-based** (Kubernetes Service DNS): `payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to a ClusterIP. kube-proxy handles routing. Simpler but less flexible.

### Eureka Server Setup

```java
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableEurekaServer
public class DiscoveryServerApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DiscoveryServerApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

```yaml
# application.yml - Eureka Server
server:
  port: 8761
eureka:
  client:
    register-with-eureka: false  # server doesn't register itself
    fetch-registry: false
  server:
    enable-self-preservation: true   # don't evict during network partition
    eviction-interval-timer-in-ms: 10000
```

### Eureka Client Registration

```yaml
# payment-service application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: payment-service   # registered name in Eureka
eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://localhost:8761/eureka/
  instance:
    lease-renewal-interval-in-seconds: 30   # heartbeat frequency
    lease-expiration-duration-in-seconds: 90  # evict if no heartbeat
    prefer-ip-address: true
```

### Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (replaces Ribbon)

```java
@Configuration
public class WebClientConfig {

    @Bean
    @LoadBalanced  // intercepts calls and resolves via registry
    public WebClient.Builder loadBalancedWebClientBuilder() {
        return WebClient.builder();
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final WebClient.Builder webClientBuilder;

    public PaymentResponse chargePayment(PaymentRequest req) {
        return webClientBuilder.build()
            .post()
            .uri("http://payment-service/api/payments")  // logical name, not IP
            .bodyValue(req)
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(PaymentResponse.class)
            .block();
    }
}
```

### Self-Preservation Mode
If Eureka server stops receiving heartbeats from many instances simultaneously (network partition), it enters **self-preservation mode** — it stops evicting entries assuming the issue is network-wide, not service death. Controlled via `enable-self-preservation: true`. Disable in dev to get fast eviction during testing.

### Client-Side vs Server-Side Load Balancing

| Approach | Client-Side (Ribbon/SCL) | Server-Side (AWS ALB, nginx) |
|----------|--------------------------|------------------------------|
| Registry fetch | Client fetches & caches | Proxy fetches |
| Latency | Lower (no extra hop) | Extra hop to LB |
| Flexibility | Custom algorithms | Fixed algorithms |
| Visibility | Client sees all instances | Opaque |
| Failure | Client handles directly | LB handles |
topics.interviewTip: When asked about Ribbon vs Spring Cloud LoadBalancer: Ribbon is in maintenance mode since 2021. Spring Cloud LoadBalancer is the modern reactive replacement. Mention that in Kubernetes environments, DNS-based discovery via kube-dns is often preferred over Eureka because the platform handles registration automatically.

topics.title: Feign Client: Interceptors, Fallbacks & Error Decoding
topics.summary: Build declarative HTTP clients with Feign — propagate auth headers via RequestInterceptor, map errors with ErrorDecoder, and integrate Resilience4j fallbacks.
topics.interviewTip: Feign runs synchronously and blocks a thread per call by default. For reactive stacks, prefer WebClient with @LoadBalanced. Also clarify the difference between Fallback (static class) and FallbackFactory (receives the cause exception) — factories are essential for logging the actual error that triggered the fallback.

topics.title: gRPC vs REST vs GraphQL in Microservices
topics.summary: Choose the right inter-service protocol: gRPC for high-throughput internal services, REST for external APIs, and GraphQL for flexible client-driven queries.
topics.interviewTip: A common interview curveball: 'Can browsers call gRPC directly?' — No, not without gRPC-Web proxy (Envoy transcodes HTTP/1.1 → gRPC HTTP/2). This limitation is why REST remains dominant for external-facing APIs. Also mention that gRPC's schema evolution (adding new fields is backward-compatible by default in proto3) is a major operational advantage over REST.

topics.title: Event-Driven Architecture: Domain Events vs Integration Events
topics.summary: Distinguish domain events (intra-bounded-context state changes) from integration events (cross-service contracts) and manage schema evolution safely.
topics.interviewTip: A great differentiator: explain @TransactionalEventListener with phase = AFTER_COMMIT. Publishing a Kafka event before the DB commits risks an inconsistency — the payment charged but the order was never persisted. The Transactional Outbox Pattern is the production-grade solution: insert the event into an 'outbox' table in the same transaction, then a relay process publishes to Kafka.

topics.title: Idempotency Keys & At-Least-Once Delivery
topics.summary: Guarantee safe retries and duplicate suppression by combining idempotency keys, DB unique constraints, and Kafka's idempotent producer semantics.
topics.interviewTip: Interviewers love: 'What's the difference between idempotent producer and exactly-once semantics in Kafka?' Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) prevents duplicates within a single producer session. Exactly-once semantics (EOS) additionally wrap the consumer-process-produce cycle in a Kafka transaction, guaranteeing the message is processed and re-published exactly once atomically. EOS requires transactional.id on the producer and isolation.level=read_committed on the consumer.

topics.title: Database-Per-Service & Data Consistency Patterns
topics.summary: Enforce microservice autonomy with database-per-service, then restore cross-service query capability via API Composition and CQRS read models.
topics.content:
## Database-Per-Service & Data Consistency Patterns

### Why Shared Database Is an Anti-Pattern

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           ANTI-PATTERN: Shared DB           │
│                                             │
│  [Order Service] ──┐                        │
│  [Payment Svc]  ───┼──► [Single PostgreSQL] │
│  [Inventory Svc]───┘         Database       │
│                                             │
│  Problems:                                  │
│  - Schema change in Orders breaks Payment  │
│  - Cannot scale each DB independently      │
│  - Coupling defeats microservice autonomy  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

With a shared DB, services are operationally decoupled but structurally coupled. A schema migration on the `orders` table requires coordinating all teams simultaneously.

### Database-Per-Service (Correct Pattern)

```
[Order Service]   ──► [Orders PostgreSQL]
[Payment Service] ──► [Payments PostgreSQL]
[Inventory Svc]   ──► [Inventory MongoDB]
[Search Service]  ──► [Elasticsearch]
```

Each service owns its schema. Teams deploy independently. Choose the right database type per service (relational, document, search index, time-series).

### Problem: Cross-Service Queries
'Show me order #123 with customer name, payment status, and stock level' spans 3 services.

**Solution 1 — API Composition**:
```java
@Service
public class OrderDashboardService {
    public OrderDashboard getOrderSummary(String orderId) {
        // Parallel calls via CompletableFuture
        CompletableFuture<Order> orderFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderClient.getOrder(orderId));
        CompletableFuture<PaymentStatus> paymentFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> paymentClient.getStatus(orderId));
        CompletableFuture<StockLevel> stockFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventoryClient.getStock(orderId));

        CompletableFuture.allOf(orderFuture, paymentFuture, stockFuture).join();

        return OrderDashboard.from(
            orderFuture.join(), paymentFuture.join(), stockFuture.join()
        );
    }
}
```
Limitation: Slow if any service is slow; no complex filtering across services.

**Solution 2 — CQRS with Materialized Read Model**:
```
[Order Events] ──► [Kafka] ──► [Dashboard Query Service]
[Payment Events]───────────►  (builds denormalized read model)
[Inventory Events]──────────► [Read DB: orders_dashboard table]
                                    │
                              [Read API: fast single-query responses]
```

The read model is eventually consistent but enables fast, complex queries without joining across services at runtime.

### Eventual Consistency Trade-offs

| Scenario | Acceptable? |
|----------|-------------|
| Product catalog freshness (5s lag) | Yes |
| Payment status after charge | Probably yes (show 'processing') |
| Bank account balance | No — needs strong consistency |
| Inventory count before purchase | Business decision: oversell or block? |

### Saga Maintains Consistency Without Shared DB
Instead of distributed transactions (2PC), each service commits locally and emits an event. If a later step fails, compensating transactions roll back earlier steps (see Saga pattern).
topics.interviewTip: A nuanced follow-up: 'How do you handle reporting that needs data from 10 services?' The answer is a dedicated reporting/analytics service that subscribes to all relevant Kafka topics and builds a denormalized reporting database (CQRS read model). This is fundamentally different from the operational query path and avoids coupling services at runtime.

topics.title: Microservices Security: JWT Propagation & OAuth2 with Keycloak
topics.summary: Secure microservices end-to-end using OAuth2 bearer token propagation, Keycloak realm setup, client credentials for service-to-service auth, and mTLS for internal channels.
topics.interviewTip: A sharp question: 'If the API Gateway validates the JWT, why does the downstream Order Service also validate it?' Defense in depth — the gateway might be bypassed in a misconfigured environment. Each service should be independently secure (zero-trust). Also: JWT validation is stateless (verify signature against JWKS + check expiry) so it's cheap — no DB lookup required.

topics.title: Spring Cloud Config & Secrets Management
topics.summary: Centralize microservice configuration with Spring Cloud Config Server, enable live reload via @RefreshScope, and manage secrets with HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.
topics.content:
## Spring Cloud Config & Secrets Management

### Why Centralized Config?
With 30 microservices each having application.yml, updating a shared database URL or feature flag requires deploying all 30 services. Config Server externalizes configuration:

```
[Git Repository]
  └── config-repo/
       ├── application.yml          (shared defaults)
       ├── order-service.yml        (service-specific)
       ├── order-service-prod.yml   (environment-specific)
       └── payment-service.yml
            │
            ▼
     [Config Server :8888]
            │
     ┌──────┴──────┐
     ▼             ▼
[Order Svc]  [Payment Svc]   (fetch config on startup)
```

### Config Server Setup

```java
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableConfigServer
public class ConfigServerApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ConfigServerApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

```yaml
# Config Server application.yml
server:
  port: 8888
spring:
  cloud:
    config:
      server:
        git:
          uri: https://github.com/myorg/config-repo
          default-label: main
          search-paths: '{application}'  # folder per service
          clone-on-start: true
          timeout: 10
```

### Client Configuration

```yaml
# order-service bootstrap.yml (loads before application context)
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  config:
    import: optional:configserver:http://config-server:8888
  profiles:
    active: prod
```

### @RefreshScope: Live Configuration Reload
Without restarting the service, push a config change and trigger reload:

```java
@RestController
@RefreshScope  // Bean is recreated when /actuator/refresh is called
public class FeatureFlagController {

    @Value("${features.new-checkout-flow.enabled:false}")
    private boolean newCheckoutEnabled;

    @GetMapping("/checkout")
    public String checkout() {
        return newCheckoutEnabled ? newCheckoutService.process() : legacyCheckout.process();
    }
}
```

Trigger refresh via Spring Cloud Bus (broadcast to all instances) or individually:
```bash
curl -X POST http://order-service:8080/actuator/refresh
# Or broadcast via Spring Cloud Bus + Kafka/RabbitMQ:
curl -X POST http://config-server:8888/actuator/busrefresh
```

### HashiCorp Vault Integration
For true secrets (database passwords, API keys), Git is inappropriate. Vault provides dynamic secrets with automatic rotation:

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    vault:
      host: vault.internal
      port: 8200
      scheme: https
      authentication: KUBERNETES  # Pod uses K8s service account token
      kubernetes:
        role: order-service
      kv:
        enabled: true
        backend: secret
        application-name: order-service
```

### AWS Secrets Manager via spring-cloud-aws
```yaml
spring:
  config:
    import: aws-secretsmanager:/prod/order-service
  cloud:
    aws:
      region:
        static: us-east-1
```

### Encrypting Properties in Git Config
Sensitive values in Git config should be encrypted (last resort — prefer Vault):
```yaml
# In config repo — encrypted value
spring:
  datasource:
    password: '{cipher}AQAoTE3qr...encryptedvalue...'
```
```bash
# Config server encrypts/decrypts using symmetric key from environment
curl http://config-server:8888/encrypt -d 'mySecretPassword'
```
topics.interviewTip: Distinguish between @RefreshScope (recreates bean on /actuator/refresh) and @ConfigurationProperties with @RefreshScope (rebinds all @Value fields). Note the gotcha: @RefreshScope on beans injected into non-refresh beans won't propagate — the outer bean caches the reference. Also mention that Spring Boot 2.4+ uses spring.config.import instead of bootstrap.yml by default.

topics.title: Microservices Testing Pyramid
topics.summary: Build a robust test suite with unit, integration (Testcontainers), consumer-driven contract (Spring Cloud Contract / Pact), and E2E tests using Docker Compose.
topics.interviewTip: Contract testing is the hardest to explain clearly — practice this: 'Contract tests verify that a producer's API meets the consumer's expectations WITHOUT running both services simultaneously. The producer generates a stub (Spring Cloud Contract) or the consumer generates a pact file (Pact framework) that is verified against the real producer in CI.' This prevents integration-test environment dependencies and catches breaking API changes before deployment.

topics.title: Service Mesh with Istio
topics.summary: Offload resilience, observability, and security concerns from application code to an Istio service mesh using Envoy sidecar proxies and declarative traffic policies.
topics.content:
## Service Mesh with Istio

### What Is a Service Mesh?
A service mesh moves cross-cutting network concerns (mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, tracing) out of application code and into an infrastructure layer:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Kubernetes Pod                   │
│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Order Service   │  │  Envoy Sidecar Proxy  │  │
│  │  (your code)     │◄─►  (injected by Istio) │  │
│  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘  │
│         All inbound/outbound traffic via Envoy   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

[Istiod Control Plane]
  - Pushes config to all Envoy sidecars
  - Issues mTLS certificates (SPIFFE/X.509)
  - Manages traffic policies
```

### mTLS Between Services (Zero-Trust)
```yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT  # All inter-pod traffic must be mutually authenticated
```
Istiod automatically provisions and rotates X.509 certificates for each pod's SPIFFE identity (`spiffe://cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/order-service`).

### Canary Deployment with Traffic Splitting
Route 5% of traffic to a new version without changing application code:
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: payment-vs
spec:
  hosts: [payment-service]
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: payment-service
        subset: v1
      weight: 95
    - destination:
        host: payment-service
        subset: v2   # canary
      weight: 5
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: payment-dr
spec:
  host: payment-service
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels: { version: v1 }
  - name: v2
    labels: { version: v2 }
```

### Circuit Breaking at Mesh Level
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
spec:
  host: inventory-service
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 50
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 10
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s    # eject unhealthy instance for 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
```

### Distributed Tracing Injection
Istio's Envoy automatically propagates `traceparent`/`b3` headers for traces. Application code only needs to forward received trace headers in outgoing calls (Istio can't do this automatically — your code must pass them through).

### When Is a Service Mesh Overkill?
- **Use Istio when**: 50+ microservices, strict security compliance (mTLS required), advanced traffic management (A/B testing, chaos engineering), polyglot services (Node.js + Java + Go can't share a Spring library).
- **Skip Istio when**: Small team, fewer than 10 services, Spring Boot monolith migrating to microservices, significant operational overhead not justified by complexity.
topics.interviewTip: Frame Istio as the infrastructure-layer equivalent of Resilience4j: 'Resilience4j implements circuit breaking in application code; Istio implements it in the network layer via Envoy. For polyglot microservices where you cannot enforce a common library, Istio is the only practical solution.' Also mention that Istio adds ~10-15ms latency per hop due to Envoy proxying — acceptable for most use cases but worth benchmarking.

topics.title: Health Checks: Readiness vs Liveness vs Startup Probes
topics.summary: Configure Kubernetes probe types correctly to avoid premature traffic routing, unnecessary restarts, and slow-start failures using Spring Boot Actuator health indicators.
topics.content:
## Health Checks: Readiness vs Liveness vs Startup Probes

### The Three Kubernetes Probe Types

```
           App starts
               │
               ▼
    ┌─ Startup Probe ──────────────────────────┐
    │  'Is the app done initializing?'         │
    │  If fails repeatedly → restart container  │
    │  Once succeeds → Liveness + Readiness    │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │ passes
       ┌───────┴──────────┐
       ▼                  ▼
  Liveness Probe     Readiness Probe
  'Should I restart?  'Send traffic now?'
  Is app stuck/dead?' Is DB connected?'
```

**Liveness Probe**: Detects deadlocks, infinite loops, or completely frozen applications. On failure: Kubernetes **restarts** the container. Should check only if the process itself is alive — NOT if downstream dependencies are healthy (that's readiness).

**Readiness Probe**: Detects whether the service can accept traffic. On failure: Kubernetes **removes the pod from the Service endpoints** (no traffic) but does NOT restart it. Should check DB connections, Kafka connectivity, cache warmup.

**Startup Probe**: Prevents liveness from killing a slow-starting application before it finishes initialization (JVM warmup, schema migrations). Disables liveness until startup succeeds.

### Spring Boot Actuator Integration

Spring Boot 2.3+ exposes liveness and readiness as separate endpoints automatically:

```yaml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true         # enables /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
      show-details: always
  health:
    livenessstate:
      enabled: true
    readinessstate:
      enabled: true
```

### Custom Health Indicator: DB Pool + Kafka Lag

```java
@Component
public class KafkaConsumerLagHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    private static final long MAX_LAG_THRESHOLD = 10_000L;

    private final KafkaConsumerLagService lagService;

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        Map<TopicPartition, Long> lags = lagService.getCurrentLag();
        long maxLag = lags.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).max().orElse(0L);

        if (maxLag > MAX_LAG_THRESHOLD) {
            return Health.down()
                .withDetail("maxLag", maxLag)
                .withDetail("threshold", MAX_LAG_THRESHOLD)
                .withDetail("message", "Consumer falling behind — mark unready")
                .build();
        }
        return Health.up().withDetail("maxLag", maxLag).build();
    }
}
```

### Kubernetes Probe Configuration

```yaml
containers:
- name: order-service
  image: order-service:1.2.0
  startupProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /actuator/health/liveness
      port: 8080
    failureThreshold: 30      # Allow 30 * 10s = 5 minutes to start
    periodSeconds: 10
  livenessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /actuator/health/liveness
      port: 8080
    initialDelaySeconds: 0    # Startup probe handles the delay
    periodSeconds: 10
    failureThreshold: 3
  readinessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /actuator/health/readiness
      port: 8080
    periodSeconds: 5
    failureThreshold: 3
```

### Common Mistakes
- **Checking dependencies in liveness**: If your downstream DB is down, liveness restarts your pod — which won't fix the DB and creates a restart loop. Liveness should be self-referential only.
- **No startup probe for slow apps**: Without a startup probe, liveness kills a JVM app during its 60-second schema migration on first boot.
- **Same endpoint for both probes**: Spring Boot's separate `/liveness` and `/readiness` endpoints exist precisely to avoid conflating these concerns.
topics.interviewTip: The most common wrong answer: 'Liveness checks if the DB is connected.' If you say this, the interviewer knows you haven't operated microservices in production. Liveness should ONLY check if the process is alive (not deadlocked). Put DB checks in Readiness. If liveness includes DB health and the DB goes down, all pods restart in a loop — making a bad situation catastrophic.

topics.title: API Versioning & Backward Compatibility
topics.summary: Evolve APIs safely using URI versioning, header versioning, additive change rules, contract testing, and structured deprecation with Sunset headers.
topics.content:
## API Versioning & Backward Compatibility

### Why API Versioning Matters
In a microservices ecosystem, multiple consumers (mobile apps, partner integrations, other services) may depend on your API. Breaking changes without versioning cause immediate production failures across all consumers simultaneously.

### Versioning Strategies

**URI Versioning** (most common, most visible):
```
GET /api/v1/orders/{id}    → returns { orderId, status, items[] }
GET /api/v2/orders/{id}    → returns { orderId, status, items[], tracking: {...} }
```

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v2/orders")
public class OrderControllerV2 {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderResponseV2 getOrder(@PathVariable String id) {
        // V2 adds tracking information
        Order order = orderService.findById(id);
        TrackingInfo tracking = trackingService.getTracking(order.getShipmentId());
        return OrderResponseV2.from(order, tracking);
    }
}
```

**Header Versioning** (cleaner URLs, harder to test in browser):
```http
GET /api/orders/123
Accept: application/vnd.myapp.v2+json
```
```java
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}",
            produces = "application/vnd.myapp.v2+json")
public OrderResponseV2 getOrderV2(@PathVariable String id) { ... }

@GetMapping(value = "/{id}",
            produces = "application/vnd.myapp.v1+json")
public OrderResponseV1 getOrderV1(@PathVariable String id) { ... }
```

### Additive vs Breaking Changes

| Change Type | Backward Compatible? | Example |
|-------------|---------------------|----------|
| Add optional field | Yes | Add `currency` to response |
| Add optional request param | Yes | Add `?includeTracking=true` |
| Remove field | **No** | Remove `shipmentId` from response |
| Rename field | **No** | `orderId` → `id` |
| Change field type | **No** | `amount: string` → `amount: number` |
| Add required field | **No** | Add required `customerId` to request |
| Change HTTP status code | **No** | 200 → 201 on creation |

### Consumer-Driven Contract Testing to Detect Breaking Changes
Pact and Spring Cloud Contract automatically detect breaking changes in CI before deployment:
```
Consumer defines expected contract → Pact Broker stores pact
→ Producer CI verifies pact against real code
→ If verification fails → PR blocked — breaking change detected early
```

### Sunset Header: Structured Deprecation
```java
@GetMapping("/api/v1/orders/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponseV1> getOrderV1(@PathVariable String id) {
    OrderResponseV1 response = orderService.getV1(id);
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .header("Deprecation", "true")
        .header("Sunset", "Sat, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT")  // RFC 7231 date
        .header("Link", "/api/v2/orders/{id}; rel=successor-version")
        .body(response);
}
```

### Deprecation Strategy Timeline
```
Month 0:  V2 released. V1 marked deprecated with Sunset header.
Month 1:  Alert consumers via email/Slack with migration guide.
Month 3:  V1 returns HTTP 301 redirecting to V2 with warning header.
Month 6:  V1 returns HTTP 410 Gone. Migration forced.
Month 9:  V1 endpoint removed from codebase.
```

### Version at the Gateway Level
Spring Cloud Gateway can route version prefixes without burdening each microservice:
```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders-v1
          uri: lb://ORDER-SERVICE-V1
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/v1/orders/**
        - id: orders-v2
          uri: lb://ORDER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/v2/orders/**
```
topics.interviewTip: When asked 'which versioning strategy do you prefer?', don't just say URI versioning — explain the trade-offs. URI versioning is the most operationally simple (works with caches, CDNs, logs, monitoring tools). Header versioning is 'purer' REST (the URL represents a resource, not a version of a resource) but harder to test manually and incompatible with many CDNs. For microservices internal APIs, consumer-driven contracts often eliminate the need for versioning altogether.

topics.title: Service Decomposition Strategies
topics.summary: Decompose a monolith into microservices using business capability mapping, DDD bounded contexts, volatility analysis, and the Strangler Fig migration pattern.
topics.content:
## Service Decomposition Strategies

### The Core Question: How Big Is a Microservice?
There is no universally correct size — decompose along lines that minimize coupling and maximize cohesion. A service that is too small creates chatty network calls; too large recreates a distributed monolith.

### Strategy 1: Decompose by Business Capability
Model services around what the business does, not technical layers:

```
E-commerce Platform Business Capabilities:
├── Product Catalog      → [Catalog Service]
├── Order Management     → [Order Service]
├── Payment Processing   → [Payment Service]
├── Inventory & Fulfillment → [Inventory Service]
├── Customer Accounts    → [Customer Service]
└── Notifications        → [Notification Service]
```

Avoid: decomposing by technical layer (Data Layer Service, Business Logic Service, UI Service) — this creates tight coupling between layers.

### Strategy 2: DDD Bounded Contexts
A bounded context is the explicit boundary within which a domain model applies. The same word 'Customer' means different things in different contexts:

```
[Order Context]          [Marketing Context]     [Support Context]
  Customer:                Customer:               Customer:
  - orderId                - loyaltyPoints         - ticketHistory
  - shippingAddress        - campaignPrefs         - satisfactionScore
  - paymentMethod          - emailOptIn            - agentAssigned
```

Don't share a single `Customer` entity across all services — each bounded context owns its own model. Integration via events or ACL.

### Strategy 3: Decompose by Volatility
Services that change together should be deployed together. Identify what changes frequently vs rarely:

```
High Volatility (deploy weekly):     Low Volatility (deploy quarterly):
- Recommendation Engine              - Core Billing Logic
- A/B Test Variants                  - Authentication
- Pricing Rules                      - Regulatory Reporting
- UI Personalization                 - Data Archival
```

### The Strangler Fig Pattern: Migrating a Monolith
Named after the strangler fig tree that grows around a host tree and eventually replaces it:

```
Phase 1:  All traffic → [Monolith]

Phase 2:  [API Gateway]
           ├─ /api/orders/** → [Order Microservice] (new)
           └─ /**            → [Monolith] (existing)

Phase 3:  [API Gateway]
           ├─ /api/orders/**  → [Order Microservice]
           ├─ /api/payments/** → [Payment Microservice]
           └─ /**             → [Monolith] (shrinking)

Phase N:  Monolith retired. All traffic to microservices.
```

### Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)
When integrating with a legacy system or third-party API with a different domain model, the ACL translates between models without polluting your clean domain:

```java
@Service
public class LegacyCRMAntiCorruptionLayer {

    public Customer translate(LegacyCRMContact legacyContact) {
        return Customer.builder()
            .id(legacyContact.getCONTACT_ID())        // camelCase from legacy
            .email(legacyContact.getEMAIL_ADDR())     // legacy column name
            .name(legacyContact.getFIRST_NM()         // legacy abbreviations
                + " " + legacyContact.getLAST_NM())
            .build();
    }
}
```

### SOLID at Service Level
- **SRP**: Each service has one reason to change (one business capability)
- **OCP**: New features via new events/APIs, not modifying existing contracts
- **LSP**: Service versions should be substitutable (backward compatibility)
- **ISP**: Don't force consumers to subscribe to events they don't need
- **DIP**: Services depend on abstractions (events, APIs) not on each other's internals
topics.interviewTip: When asked 'how would you break up this monolith?', walk through all three strategies systematically: (1) identify business capabilities, (2) find bounded contexts where the same entity means different things, (3) analyze volatility to prioritize which to extract first. Then mention the Strangler Fig as the safe migration path — extracting one capability at a time with the gateway routing to both old and new simultaneously.

topics.title: Async Communication Patterns in Microservices
topics.summary: Choose the right async messaging pattern — fire-and-forget, request-reply with correlation IDs, or pub-sub — and know when sync REST/gRPC beats Kafka.
topics.interviewTip: The best candidates can articulate WHY to choose async: 'We made the notification service async because a slow email provider should never block a user's checkout — the checkout response time would degrade. Payment, however, stays synchronous because users need immediate confirmation of whether their card was charged.' Frame every async decision in terms of the user experience and failure isolation impact.

topics.title: SLI, SLO, SLA & Error Budgets
topics.summary: Define measurable reliability targets with SLIs and SLOs, calculate error budgets, and implement Prometheus burn rate alerts to proactively protect uptime.
topics.content:
## SLI, SLO, SLA & Error Budgets

### The Reliability Hierarchy

```
  SLA (Service Level Agreement)
  └─ Legal/contractual commitment to customers
     └─ SLO (Service Level Objective)
        └─ Internal engineering target (stricter than SLA)
           └─ SLI (Service Level Indicator)
              └─ The actual metric you measure
```

### SLI: Service Level Indicator
A quantitative measure of service behavior. Good SLIs directly reflect user experience:

- **Availability**: `(successful requests) / (total requests)`
- **Latency**: `(requests served < 300ms) / (total requests)` (p99)
- **Error rate**: `(5xx responses) / (total responses)`
- **Throughput**: requests per second processed
- **Freshness**: age of newest data in a cache/read model

### SLO: Service Level Objective
The target value for an SLI over a time window. Defines what 'reliable enough' means for engineering:

```
SLO Examples:
  Availability: 99.9% of requests succeed over a 30-day rolling window
  Latency p99:  95% of requests complete in < 500ms
  Error rate:   < 0.1% of requests return 5xx
```

**99.9% availability = how much downtime per year?**
```
100% - 99.9% = 0.1% allowed failure time
0.001 × 365 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes = 525.6 minutes = ~8.7 hours/year
0.001 × 30 days × 24h × 60m = 43.2 minutes downtime per month

Common SLO targets:
  99%    → 87.6 hours/year  (~3.65 days)
  99.9%  → 8.76 hours/year  (~43 min/month)
  99.95% → 4.38 hours/year  (~22 min/month)
  99.99% → 52.6 min/year    (~4.4 min/month)
```

### Error Budget
Error budget = 1 - SLO. It's the allowed failure capacity before breaching the SLO:

```
SLO: 99.9% availability
Error Budget: 0.1% = 43.2 minutes/month

Budget consumed:                Budget remaining:
  Week 1: 20min incident  →    23.2 minutes left
  Week 2: 5min blip       →    18.2 minutes left
  Week 3: 25min outage    →    -6.8 minutes (BUDGET EXCEEDED)
  → Freeze feature releases until next month
  → Focus 100% on reliability improvements
```

### Prometheus SLO Recording Rules

```yaml
# prometheus/rules/order-service-slo.yml
groups:
- name: order-service-slo
  interval: 30s
  rules:
  # SLI: availability over 5-minute window
  - record: job:request_availability:rate5m
    expr: |
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="order-service", code!~"5.."}[5m]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="order-service"}[5m]))
```

### Burn Rate Alerts
A burn rate of 1x means you're consuming your error budget exactly at the rate where you'll exhaust it by the end of the window. A burn rate of 14.4x means you'll exhaust the entire monthly budget in 2 hours:

```yaml
  # Alert when burn rate is too fast (will exhaust budget early)
  - alert: OrderServiceHighErrorBurnRate
    expr: |
      (
        sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="order-service",code=~"5.."}[1h]))
        /
        sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="order-service"}[1h]))
      ) > 14.4 * 0.001   # 14.4x burn rate on 99.9% SLO
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Order service burning error budget 14.4x faster than sustainable"
      description: "At this rate, the monthly error budget will be exhausted in 2 hours"
```

### SLA vs SLO: Key Difference
**SLO** is an internal engineering target. Typically stricter than the SLA to provide a safety buffer:
- **SLO**: 99.95% (internal target — engineers get paged)
- **SLA**: 99.9% (contractual — customers get SLA credits if breached)

The gap (0.05%) is the safety margin. If the SLO is breached, engineers act before the SLA is breached and customers are impacted.

references.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives
Alerting on SLOs — Google SRE Workbook

topics.interviewTip: Walk through the error budget math confidently: '99.9% SLO on a 30-day window gives us 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime. When we deploy a risky feature and it causes a 20-minute incident, we've burned 46% of our monthly budget — at that point we slow feature releases and prioritize reliability.' Interviewers from SRE-mature companies (Google, Netflix, Spotify) will love that you can connect reliability metrics to engineering velocity decisions.
